chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan, from Amr ibn Saeed, from Musaddaq ibn Sadaqa, from Ammar ibn Musa, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
I asked him about the one in Ihram eating the citron. He said: 'Yes'. I said to him, 'Its smell is aromatic.' He said: 'The citron is food. It is not from the perfumes.'

key_terms.الْمُحْرِمِ: The person in the state of Ihram

ai.seo_question: Does eating a citron break the Ihram due to its smell?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the distinction between food and perfume by citing the citron (utrugg), ruling that its pleasant scent does not invalidate Ihram because it is primarily consumed as food. This hadith highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle that the classification of an item depends on its primary use and nature, rather than solely on its sensory attributes. It provides a practical legal precedent for distinguishing between incidental scents and intentional perfume usage during pilgrimage.

en.hubeali:
Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Muhammad Bin Ahmad, from Ahmad Bin Al Hassan, from Amro Bin Saeed, from Musaddaq Bin Sadaqa, from Ammar Bin Musa, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup>, said, ‘
I asked himasws about the one in Ihraam eating the citron. Heasws said: ‘Yes’. I said to himasws, ‘Its smell is aromatic’. Heasws said: ‘The citron is food. It is not from the perfumes’.
en.sarwar: 16. Muhammad ibn Yahya has narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ahmad ibn al-Hassan from ‘Amr ibn Sa‘id from Musaddiq ibn Sadaqah from ‘Ammar ibn Musa who has said the following:

“I once asked abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, about a man who is in the state of Ihram and eats citron. He (the Imam) said, ‘Yes, he can eat.’ I then said, ‘It has nice fragrance.’ He (the Imam) said, ‘Citron is food and it is not a fragrance.’”
